captions.text: A cycle brings the same states back in the same order.
Track where a full cycle ends and how many extra steps
you take.
When all you need is a last digit, you can multiply
last digits and leave the rest of the number behind.
AMC Upper Primary practice can use a repeating picture,
a clock or the last digit of a large power.
Write a small first cycle.
A Mawa style investigation can change the base or the
number of steps.
Check whether the cycle length stays the same.
It is nine o'clock on a twelve-hour clock.
What number will the hour hand point to after seventeen
hours?
Start by removing any whole turns that bring you back
to the same place.
Every twelve hours returns to the starting number.
The seventeen hours leave five extra hours after full
turns.
Step five hours ahead.
Wrap past twelve if needed, so the hour hand points to
two.
What is the units digit of three to the power
thirty-seven?
Work with just the units digits of its first few
powers.
Watch for the first repeat.
A remainder of zero will need a careful interpretation.
The first four units digits are three, nine, seven and
one.
The next digit repeats the first, and the same
multiplication rule gives the same later digits.
The exponent thirty-seven leaves a remainder of one on
division by four.
Use position one in the cycle.
The digit at that position is three.
If the remainder is zero, the fourth position sits at
the end of the last full cycle.
Add the first fifty-one positive powers of three,
starting with exponent one.
What is the units digit of the sum?
You already know the cycle of the last digits.
Work out what one whole block contributes to the sum.
One full cycle has units digits three, nine, seven and
one.
Their sum is twenty, with units digit zero.
There are twelve full cycles and three terms left.
Every completed block contributes zero to the units
digit.
Add the first three digits of the cycle.
Their sum is nineteen, so the final units digit is
nine.
The units digit of a sum depends only on the units
digits of the addends.
Tens contributed by any full cycle cannot change it.
The answer is nine.
Check that the tail starts at exponent one of a new
cycle, because the last completed block ended at a
multiple of four.
If the step count is a multiple of the cycle length,
land on the last listed item when the cycle was
numbered from one.
For a sum, add the contributions of the earlier terms
as well as the final term.
Check the total contributed by each full cycle.
Record states in order.
Find the first state you can recognise again, and count
the length from one occurrence to the next.
Divide by the cycle length and use the remainder.
